video_title: AI researchers debate how close we are to recursive self-improvement
gist: Three AI researchers (Beren Millidge of Zyphra, John Schulman of Thinking Machines, Charlie O'Neill of Baseten) debate with Dwarkesh Patel whether recursive self-improvement is close, concluding that automating AI research is effectively ASI-complete, that RL's power comes from a tiny number of extremely high-signal bits layered on mid-training, and that distillation (via Chinese router-proxy services and cheap logit-copying) is the main force preventing model-provider centralization.

insights.claim: The most likely technical reason AI does not produce transformative superintelligence by 2036 is a Moravec's-paradox-style failure to generalize: models keep acing benchmarks and environments (math, chess-like tasks) without ever developing the generalized meta-learning and continual-learning ability needed to compound into real-world autonomy.
insights.speaker: guest, AI researcher
insights.so_what: If this bottleneck holds, expect capability progress to keep showing repeated 'this is AGI... no it's not' hype cycles rather than a discrete takeoff, which argues against pricing in near-term explosive productivity gains from AI.
insights.quote: If somehow that continues, and there's never the true spark of generalization that occurs, I think that could lead to the AI just being extremely good at everything that people put into a benchmark.

insights.claim: AI capability relative to humans behaves like chess-engine Elo: a smooth linear rise that produces little visible economic impact until it crosses the human expert range, after which impact becomes abrupt and total (as with chess engines going from 'humans sometimes win' to 'humans never win').
insights.speaker: guest, AI researcher
insights.so_what: The panel believes current LLMs are already close to crossing this human-Elo threshold in several domains, implying the modest measured economic impact of AI so far could flip discontinuously in the near term rather than staying gradual.
insights.quote: We're already pretty close, in my opinion, to where we'll start crossing the human Elo score.

insights.claim: Only two scenarios plausibly prevent a 2036 superintelligence outcome: an asymptote in generalization hit just before crossing human-level performance, or heavy exogenous AI regulation — and the panel views regulation as the more likely of the two.
insights.speaker: guest, AI researcher
insights.so_what: Investors modeling tail risk to AI capex/timelines should weight policy/regulatory risk more heavily than a pure technical-plateau scenario.
insights.quote: The only other way is there's some dramatic regulation on AI. This is what I see as the most likely way for this scenario to happen.

insights.claim: The key open question for rapid RSI is not raw intelligence but whether AIs can learn to propose their own research objectives and sustain a self-propelling improve-propose-improve loop without going off the rails — current models are much better at executing a given experiment than at deciding which experiment to run.
insights.speaker: guest, AI researcher
insights.so_what: Watch AI-research-agent products for evidence of autonomous objective-setting (not just autonomous coding/execution) as the real leading indicator of takeoff risk, rather than coding benchmark scores.
insights.quote: How well can AIs generalize to learning their own objectives? ... To have any kind of self-propelling automated loop, we need the AI to propose objectives, optimize them, figure that out, propose a new objective.

insights.claim: Defining objectives and deciding 'what we actually want' (alignment, constitutions, model specs) is the human job most likely to persist the longest even after AI automates the technical work of AI research itself.
insights.speaker: John Schulman, Chief Scientist, Thinking Machines
insights.so_what: Post-training/alignment teams and the human-judgment layer of AI labs are a durable moat and cost center even in a highly automated-R&D future — relevant for valuing labs' organizational structure, not just compute.
insights.quote: I would say that the last job for humans... is defining the objective and deciding what we actually want... Alignment is the final job.

insights.claim: Tasks split into 'cumulative' ones (like RSI/AI research, where each discovery like attention, MoE, or GRPO is permanently locked in and never has to be re-derived) versus 'non-stationary' ones (like being a law-firm paralegal, where context and relationships constantly change) — and RSI is unfortunately the easier of the two for current AI.
insights.speaker: guest, AI researcher
insights.so_what: This predicts labs will keep funneling disproportionate compute and effort into AI-research automation (the 'easy' cumulative task) rather than into general knowledge-worker automation, reinforcing an AI-research-first capital allocation thesis for the labs.
insights.quote: It's so unfortunate that RSI happened to be easier than being a paralegal.

insights.claim: Models are plausibly a millionfold less sample-efficient than humans, comparing the data a human sees from birth to adulthood against the data a model sees from cold start to the end of training — and this sample-inefficiency, if it doesn't transfer well from simulation to real-world long-horizon tasks (running a business, day-trading, winning a court case), could be the deeper structural blocker to fast RSI.
insights.speaker: Dwarkesh Patel, host
insights.so_what: This is the single biggest wildcard for RSI timelines the panel identifies: if weight-update sample efficiency doesn't improve, real-world-embedded superintelligence claims (running companies, trading, litigation) should be discounted far more heavily than pure-reasoning capability claims.
insights.quote: They're plausibly a millionfold behind humans in terms of how much data a human sees from birth to adulthood versus how much a model sees from cold start to finishing training.

themes.theme: Distillation and the collapsing model-provider moat

insights.claim: Distillation is the primary force preventing consolidation among frontier model providers, because anything a model learns via RL is a small number of bits and can be cheaply copied by generating trajectories from the target model and training on them.
insights.speaker: guest, AI researcher
insights.so_what: Argues against a durable technical moat for frontier labs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) on capability alone — pricing power will need to come from distribution, brand, enterprise integration, or proprietary deployment data rather than raw model quality.
insights.quote: I think distillation is the main thing that fights against the centralizing force. Basically anything that can be learned through RL can be distilled very easily, because it's a small number of bits.

insights.claim: Chinese AI companies reportedly obtain high-quality prompt-distribution training data via router/proxy services that let mainland users access blocked US frontier models (mostly for coding), with these services collecting and selling the resulting query data — giving Chinese labs a distillation shortcut on exactly the realistic prompt distribution they need.
insights.speaker: guest, AI researcher
insights.so_what: This is a concrete, actionable data-supply-chain mechanism explaining how Chinese open-weight models (GLM, Kimi, DeepSeek) keep pace with US frontier labs despite export controls — relevant to any thesis about compute-export-control efficacy or the US/China AI capability gap.
insights.quote: There are all these router or proxy services that allow people in China to use these models, mostly for coding. And these router services are collecting and selling some of the data.

insights.claim: Anthropic's Sonnet 5 and Opus 5 reportedly underperform Chinese open models GLM-5.3 and Kimi K3 despite Anthropic having proprietary RL environments and full logit-distillation access to its own frontier model — suggesting frontier labs may have little durable advantage in RL-environment quality, and that real-world deployment/user data matters more than in-house environments.
insights.speaker: guest, AI researcher
insights.so_what: If proprietary RL environments aren't the moat, then the market should re-rate the value of labs' historical RLHF/environment IP relative to their live user base and deployment telemetry as the real differentiator.
insights.quote: Isn't it weird how Sonnet 5 and Opus 5 are almost objectively worse models than GLM-5.3 and Kimi K3, even though they've had access to not only distillation but logit distillation from Mythos?

insights.claim: Frontier and Chinese labs largely purchase training data from the same commercial data vendors, so the pretraining data advantage of US labs over Chinese competitors is thinner than commonly assumed.
insights.speaker: guest, AI researcher
insights.so_what: Undercuts a 'data moat' thesis for US labs; competitive advantage has to come from compute scale, RLHF taste, or deployment-data flywheels rather than raw dataset access.
insights.quote: The frontier AI labs buy all their data from big data companies. The Chinese can also just buy the same data from data companies... if they have exactly the same data and they can buy that, they can also distill.

insights.claim: RL-environment quality has two separable axes — difficulty ('benchmaxxing') and realism — and naive distillation only transfers the benchmaxxable capabilities well; without a rich realistic/multi-turn prompt distribution, distilled student models match teacher benchmarks but underperform on messy real-world tasks, which may explain why smaller distilled models sometimes disappoint despite strong benchmark scores.
insights.speaker: guest, AI researcher
insights.so_what: Investors evaluating a smaller/cheaper model release should discount benchmark scores as a quality signal and weight real-user feedback and agentic multi-turn evals more heavily.
insights.quote: If you only have this distribution of easily verifiable tasks, then you can match the big model on all the benchmarks, but you do worse on this broader distribution.

insights.claim: It is much easier for a distiller to elicit a specific behavior (e.g., 'be a good politician') from an existing frontier model than for the original frontier lab to build that capability from scratch, because the frontier model can generate near-infinite realistic training traces on demand once the capability exists anywhere.
insights.speaker: guest, AI researcher
insights.so_what: Reinforces that being second-to-market with a distilled model is structurally cheaper and faster than being first, which should compress margins for pioneering labs over time.
insights.quote: It's actually much easier to say, 'I want something like this,' and then get the AI to produce a billion variations, than to actually create the thing like this to begin with.

insights.claim: In a controlled grid study (pairing every open pretraining recipe from 2019-present with every dataset from 2019-present, run with Jerry Han at Princeton), better data explained roughly a 12x compute-efficiency gain to reach a given capability level, versus roughly 3.7x from architecture improvements, at small scale.
insights.speaker: guest, AI researcher
insights.so_what: For anyone modeling future frontier-model cost curves, data curation/synthesis investment may deserve more capital allocation weight than architecture R&D, at least at the scales tested.
insights.quote: You see that the data seems to explain something like a 12.0x compute efficiency gain, but the architecture improvements explain something like a 3.7x compute efficiency gain, at a very small scale.

insights.claim: Architecture improvements (e.g., GQA enabling million-token context cheaply) often act as unlocks that make certain data usable at all, rather than pure multiplicative efficiency gains — so isolating 'data vs. architecture' contribution at a fixed small context length understates architecture's true importance.
insights.speaker: guest, AI researcher
insights.so_what: Simple efficiency-gain attribution studies (like the 12x-vs-3.7x data point above) may be systematically biased toward data, so should be treated as a floor on architecture's real contribution.
insights.quote: If we didn't have even GQA... it would be ridiculously expensive to do a million context. Because of that, we could never use the data which is actually at a million context, so we couldn't get these capabilities.

insights.claim: The low-hanging fruit in pretraining data quality is largely exhausted, since useful internet content is not growing at the historical pace of past data-curation gains; expect diminishing, smaller loss-drop improvements from data going forward rather than a repeat of past multi-hundred-x compute-efficiency gains.
insights.speaker: guest, AI researcher
insights.so_what: Argues against extrapolating historical data-driven efficiency curves (e.g., Epoch's ~3x/year estimate) forward indefinitely; expect compute scaling and RL/post-training to carry more of the future improvement burden.
insights.quote: We've probably got a bunch of 0.1% loss drops to go, but definitely not as many as have currently occurred.

insights.claim: Signal for pretraining tasks already exists abundantly in Common Crawl (the challenge is filtering noise), but for frontier post-training/reasoning tasks the needed signal simply does not exist anywhere in scraped data — there is no hidden proof of a Millennium Prize problem sitting in Common Crawl to filter for — so further gains must come directly from humans or constructed environments.
insights.speaker: guest, AI researcher
insights.so_what: Explains why RL-environment construction (not data scraping/filtering) is becoming the critical, defensible input for frontier capability — an argument for valuing environment/RLHF-data companies (e.g., Mercor, Scale-style vendors) as a structural bottleneck business.
insights.quote: There's no hidden proof of a Millennium Prize problem sitting in Common Crawl that we can just filter until we see it.

insights.claim: Building useful RL environments follows a ladder where each successive rung of difficulty requires exponentially more effort to construct, because labs currently exploit an asymmetry (it's easier to define a complex hidden generative process and verify against it than to build a genuinely long, complex real-world-like task) that runs out as task realism/horizon increases.
insights.speaker: guest, AI researcher
insights.so_what: Predicts a coming slowdown in visible capability jumps as environment-construction costs rise faster than compute costs fall — a check against naive extrapolation of recent RL-driven capability gains.
insights.quote: I think it's just going to hit diminishing returns at some point, diminishing returns in how hard it is to create those environments in the first place.

insights.claim: A model pretrained only on data up to 1930 (the 'Talkie' model) was fine-tuned on modern coding-agent data and outperformed Claude 3 Opus on SWE-bench, showing that once correct expert behavior examples exist, they can be surprisingly easy to instill even into a base model with zero prior domain exposure.
insights.speaker: guest, AI researcher
insights.so_what: Suggests capability transfer via targeted fine-tuning/distillation is more powerful than raw pretraining scale for narrow skills — relevant to how cheaply competitors can catch up on specific benchmarks.
insights.quote: This model that has no knowledge of code whatsoever can be fine-tuned on a moderate amount of data and behave better as a coding agent than this much larger pre-trained model, which is pretty crazy.

insights.claim: A counter-example shows RL curricula fail when the gap between rungs is too large: a model pretrained only up to fifth-grade math/primary-school English could not be RL'd directly to late-high-school/college math, but could climb successfully when trained rung-by-rung (year 7, then year 8, etc.) — confirming RL's core limitation is poor exploration when correct answers are far outside the current policy's reach.
insights.speaker: guest, AI researcher
insights.so_what: Predicts labs will keep needing dense, incrementally-staged environment curricula (not one-shot jumps to frontier difficulty) to keep RL gains coming, which is a real cost/time constraint on capability roadmaps.
insights.quote: If the model can't get it in 128 rollouts, it's very unlikely to get signal to progress. This is why in RL we need curricula, whereas in pre-training we don't.

insights.claim: Frontier active-parameter counts (e.g., for OpenAI's and Anthropic's models, referred to in the conversation by the placeholder name 'Mythos') are likely much smaller than the widely rumored ~10-trillion-parameter range, based on comparison with known open-source model scales.
insights.speaker: guest, AI researcher
insights.so_what: Pushes back on market narratives that frontier model quality is primarily a function of ever-larger parameter counts, implying compute is increasingly spent on RL rollouts/training tokens rather than raw model size.
insights.quote: I have a feeling that Mythos and the GPT models are much smaller than the 10 trillion parameter range that people are talking about.

insights.claim: Frontier model parameter-count growth is likely to plateau or slow over the next few years (rather than continuing a ~2x/year pace) because RL rollout inference-efficiency needs push toward smaller active-parameter models, with total-parameter scaling instead gated by hardware memory bandwidth/VRAM (H100 vs. GB200/Vera Rubin generations).
insights.speaker: guest, AI researcher
insights.so_what: Implies near-term frontier model economics favor smaller, cheaper-to-serve models optimized for RL throughput; watch next-gen GPU memory bandwidth (Vera Rubin generation) as the unlock for a return to larger, undersaturated models.
insights.quote: Inference efficiency is super important for RL rollouts. This will really push down active parameters quite a lot.

themes.theme: Why RL works better than expected

insights.claim: Mid-training (pretraining on synthetic reasoning data and warm-start environments) does roughly 80% of the work toward a model's final RL-checkpoint performance; RL itself only tweaks the policy with a small number of very high-signal bits on top.
insights.speaker: Beren Millidge, CTO, Zyphra
insights.so_what: Investors should attribute recent leaps in model quality more to mid-training/synthetic-data pipelines than to the RL algorithm itself when evaluating which labs/vendors have a genuine edge.
insights.quote: What is slightly underestimated is the mid-training... This takes the model almost 80% of the way to the final RL checkpoint often.

insights.claim: RL is dramatically more sample-efficient than SFT because it only back-propagates a single correct/incorrect bit per episode, whereas SFT forces the model to match every intermediate reasoning token of a teacher trace — diluting the true 'did you get it right' signal in noise.
insights.speaker: Beren Millidge, CTO, Zyphra
insights.so_what: Explains why RL-based post-training pipelines (used by all frontier labs) outperform pure SFT-on-traces approaches and why RL compute is worth paying for despite its small per-episode bit count.
insights.quote: For RL, you only get the one bit. That means that signal is not drowned out in the noise of all the other bits the model has. It's really a super dramatic increase in the signal-to-noise ratio.

insights.claim: RL did not produce much cross-domain ('horizontal') reasoning transfer — training on math doesn't make a model the best coder, you still need code-specific RL — but it did produce strong 'horizon generalization': models trained on progressively longer tasks learn to sustain effort and make progress on entirely new long-horizon tasks.
insights.speaker: guest, AI researcher
insights.so_what: Suggests future capability investment should target task-horizon/persistence training broadly rather than assuming domain-specific reasoning gains will transfer automatically across verticals.
insights.quote: I don't think we necessarily got this horizontal generalization... I think what we did get, though, is horizon generalization.

insights.claim: EdgeBench data shows the length of task models can successfully work on is doubling roughly every three months, offered as concrete evidence of real RL-driven horizon generalization rather than pure benchmark overfitting.
insights.speaker: guest, AI researcher
insights.so_what: A trackable, quantifiable leading indicator for AI-agent capability progress that investors can monitor release-over-release, arguably more informative than static benchmark leaderboards.
insights.quote: There was a paper called EdgeBench which showed that the rate at which models can work for longer is doubling every three months.

insights.claim: The observed 'entropy collapse' in RL-trained models (repetitive writing styles, reused character names, reduced output diversity) is a byproduct of exploiting simple/narrow reward judges rather than a fundamental limitation of RL as a method — the AlphaGo-style capacity for creative, non-human-initialized solutions (e.g., zero-day exploits found by models in the OpenAI-Hugging Face sandbox incident) shows RL/LLMs can still be highly creative when environments are diverse.
insights.speaker: guest, AI researcher
insights.so_what: Reframes 'AI writing all sounds the same' complaints as a fixable reward-model/judge-diversity problem rather than a hard ceiling on machine creativity, which matters for creative-industry disruption timelines.
insights.quote: This is really a problem with the judge. It's not a problem with RL in general.

insights.claim: Because so many open-weight labs are distilling primarily from Claude, most open-weight models now write in the same style and share the same stylistic 'tics' as Claude, creating an emerging content monoculture across the open-source LLM ecosystem.
insights.speaker: guest, AI researcher
insights.so_what: A concrete, observable market signal: expect declining stylistic differentiation among open-weight model outputs, which is a risk for AI-content-detection products and for platforms relying on stylistic diversity.
insights.quote: So many people are distilling, mostly from Claude, that all the open-weight models write the same way as Claude and have the same tics. This seems kind of concerning to me.

themes.theme: Continual learning and the 'hive mind' deployment loop

insights.claim: A crude version of learning from billions of deployed model instances is already happening today — not via live weight updates, but by feeding filtered/annotated deployment traces back into the pretraining or mid-training data for the next model generation.
insights.speaker: guest, AI researcher
insights.so_what: Generation-over-generation model improvement is partly a data-flywheel effect, not pure algorithmic progress — labs with the largest active user bases (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini) have a compounding advantage independent of research talent.
insights.quote: Right now, you can obviously take your deployment data and put this in the pre-train or the mid-train of future models... I think it explains quite a bit.

insights.claim: Chinese AI companies reportedly train directly on deployment data obtained by pinging Western frontier models via proxy services, while Western labs claim not to train on user data (though it likely still feeds in indirectly) — giving Chinese developers a more direct version of the deployment-data flywheel.
insights.speaker: guest, AI researcher
insights.so_what: A regulatory/policy angle: Western labs' self-imposed restraint on training on user data may be a competitive disadvantage relative to Chinese labs with fewer such constraints.
insights.quote: But the Chinese 100% do. They definitely get this advantage. This is basically what distillation is.

insights.claim: Cursor's Composer coding model runs genuine online reinforcement learning from live user signal (not just the old autocomplete 'Tab' model but the full generative model), using REINFORCE-style updates from single, ungrouped user interactions and validating each new checkpoint against CursorBench before deploying a new model roughly every five hours (discarding it if it doesn't improve).
insights.speaker: guest, AI researcher
insights.so_what: Cursor/Composer is a live, concrete example of a company-specific continual-learning loop already in production, ahead of the frontier labs' theoretical roadmaps — a template that other vertical AI-coding/agent companies (and their investors) can benchmark against.
insights.quote: Their solution to whether it got worse or not was that if it improved on CursorBench, they would deploy the new model every five hours. If it didn't, they would throw that version out.

insights.claim: Whether AI models achieve a rapid 'hive mind' style learning loop from all deployment experience is mostly an incentives/business question, not a technical one: enterprises will resist letting a shared foundation model absorb weight updates from their proprietary usage data, pushing the industry toward modular add-ons (LoRAs, compressed 'cartridges'/KV-caches) that specialize a model without altering the shared base.
insights.speaker: guest, AI researcher
insights.so_what: Points to a growing market for per-customer model-adapter infrastructure (LoRA-serving, cartridge/KV-cache compression platforms) as enterprises resist sharing their proprietary interaction data with foundation-model providers.
insights.quote: Companies aren't going to want to have the model provider learn from all of their deployment, because that might just reduce the advantage of their business.

insights.claim: Naive continual fine-tuning of a live deployed model (via repeated SFT or even on-policy distillation on successful traces) reliably causes catastrophic forgetting and degraded general capability after enough iterative micro-updates; RL causes smaller, less destructive weight perturbations but is correspondingly limited in how much new explicit knowledge it can inject, which is why labs still periodically retrain new base models from scratch rather than perpetually updating one model.
insights.speaker: Charlie O'Neill, Head of Model Training, Baseten
insights.so_what: This is a real technical ceiling on the 'model that never stops learning' vision — expect discrete model-generation retraining cycles (not seamless continuous learning) to remain the norm for the next several years, which has direct implications for compute-cost forecasting.
insights.quote: If I SFT the model on just successful traces... eventually in the very iterative regime, when you're doing hundreds of these micro-updates, you see catastrophic forgetting.

themes.theme: Timelines: remote workers, 10x uplift, and ASI

insights.claim: A true drop-in AI 'remote worker' capable of full computer use and month-long autonomous, multi-stakeholder projects across white-collar domains (not just coding, but legal, video editing, paralegal work) is plausible within about 1 year if it doesn't require browser-only interaction, but likely takes closer to 3 years for full generality including legacy/browser-based systems, with organizations restructuring workflows to be AI-legible closing much of that gap sooner.
insights.speaker: guest, AI researcher
insights.so_what: A concrete, near-term (1-3 year) timeline for AI-native white-collar labor substitution that investors can use to underwrite staffing/BPO disruption theses and agent-tooling company valuations.
insights.quote: If it's not browser-based—it can send Slack messages, it can do all this stuff—I'd still probably say around a year.

insights.claim: AI agents already handle real multi-step bureaucratic tasks end-to-end: one guest reported using Codex to autonomously gather all tax documents (including navigating multiple web portals) and send them to an accountant, executing the task perfectly.
insights.speaker: guest, AI researcher
insights.so_what: A tangible current-state proof point that agentic AI is already displacing certain categories of white-collar admin/paralegal work today, not just in forecasts.
insights.quote: This year, I literally just told Codex to go get everything I needed and send it to the accountant... It did it. It was perfect.

insights.claim: A persistent behavioral weakness of current and near-future AI agents is a lack of interpersonal forcefulness — models are 'too nice' to do things like push back on or pressure a colleague to get something done, which will remain a gap even as technical task automation improves.
insights.speaker: guest, AI researcher
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific, durable niche for human labor (interpersonal pressure/negotiation/management) that will likely resist automation even after most cognitive-task automation is solved.
insights.quote: An example of something that it wouldn't be good at is if I have to yell at someone to get something at work, or really push someone to get something done. The model just isn't going to do that.

insights.claim: Panelists' estimates for a 10x productivity uplift specifically for AI researchers (as opposed to generic white-collar remote workers) ranged from about 2 years to 5-10 years — notably longer than their 1-3 year estimate for generic white-collar remote-worker automation — because AI-research uplift is bottlenecked on delegating judgment about which experiments to run, not just code execution.
insights.speaker: guest, AI researcher
insights.so_what: Counterintuitively, the panel views automating AI research itself as harder than automating typical knowledge work, which should temper the most aggressive 'imminent intelligence explosion' narratives built on recursive AI-research automation.
insights.quote: Somewhere between 5-10 years?... Really, you think it's longer than for a general remote worker? Interesting.

insights.claim: An AI that dominates top human experts across every computer-based cognitive field (essentially ASI) was estimated at 3-4 years by one panelist and 5-10 years by others, with automating AI research itself viewed as effectively 'ASI-complete' — requiring solved long-horizon/continual learning, not just more context length, because context windows in the low millions of tokens are insufficient for some real-world domains (e.g., becoming a superhuman TSMC process engineer).
insights.speaker: guest, AI researcher
insights.so_what: Gives investors a range (3-10 years) directly from AI researchers themselves for full ASI-level capability, with the AI-research-automation subcase treated as the hardest and most consequential milestone to watch for a true intelligence explosion.
insights.quote: So basically, you think automating AI research is ASI-complete or something? Yeah, I think so.
